paras: The lynching of Gus Mentzel and C. D. R. Bradley took place in Raton, New Mexico Territory, in late June 1882, when citizens hanged the gambler Mentzel and then his partner Bradley. Mentzel was seized immediately after he was reported to have shot three men dead and wounded several others, including two deputy sheriffs, while resisting arrest. The story ran as a telegraph item in papers from New York to California, framed as a tale of a murderous gambler punished by an enraged town.

According to a dispatch from Raton dated June 26, Deputy Sheriff Dolman tried that afternoon to arrest Mentzel, who was described as a gambler who kept a gambling house. Mentzel fired two shots, slightly wounding Dolman and two men standing nearby, Charles Fox and Jacob Harris.

Shortly afterward Dolman made a second attempt at Mentzel's gambling house, and Mentzel again opened fire. Justice of the Peace Harry Moulton, Hugh Edelston, one of the proprietors of the Moulton Hotel, and the saloon-keeper S. H. Jackson were reported instantly killed, and H. Latimer and Deputy Sheriff Bergan were seriously wounded. The Evening Critic's shorter dispatch placed the shooting at the Moulton Hotel and called the three dead "merely bystanders."

Immediately after the killing, Mentzel was seized by what the dispatch called "the enraged citizens" and hanged to the sign of the Raton Bank. A later bulletin said Bergan was dying, that the citizens were "wild with excitement," and that a raid on the town's gamblers was expected that night. A second Raton dispatch, dated June 28, reported that after Mentzel's lynching "the crowd took his pal, C. D. R. Bradley, and hanged him." No report gave any act by Bradley beyond being Mentzel's partner; a Dakota weekly said he was "strangled by a rope prepared by the citizens of Raton."
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution for either hanging appears in the coverage, and no follow-up confirmed whether Bergan died or whether the expected raid on gamblers took place.

The first account ran on June 27 in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union under the headline "Bloody Affray—Three Men Killed and Others Wounded—The Murderer Lynched." A version credited to the Denver Tribune appeared the next day in the Portland Daily Press as "Gambling and Murder" and in the New-York Tribune as "Hanged for Killing," and the Arizona Weekly Citizen reprinted it on July 2. In Washington the Evening Critic headed its brief "A Mexican Murderer Mobbed," the only report to attach an ethnic label to Mentzel.

The Bradley bulletin, which called Mentzel "the sanguinary gambler," ran from June 29 to 30 in Memphis, Rock Island, Wheeling, Richmond, Sacramento, Seattle and Salt Lake City. Its headlines treated the second hanging lightly: "Followed His Pal," "Served His Partner Likewise," "Bad Place for Gamblers" and "Double Lynching." Weekly summaries in early July compressed the story into a sentence or two, and none of the papers commented on the lynchings or criticized the crowd.

The detailed Raton dispatch named three dead, while the Richmond Dispatch and the Hand County Press said Mentzel killed four men and the Lake Charles Echo said "four of the sheriff's posse were killed." The later figure may have counted the dying Bergan, but no report of his death was found. The Huntsville Gazette alone said Mentzel was hanged "to a sign over the Third National Bank" rather than the Raton Bank.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Citizens seized the gambler Gus Mentzel right after he shot several men while resisting arrest and hanged him to a bank sign, then hanged his partner Bradley [A2][A8][A14].

'Enraged citizens' or 'a mob' seized Mentzel and hanged him without any legal process in reprisal for the killings, and 'the crowd' then hanged his partner Bradley [A2][A3][A8][A14]. The papers do not identify either man as Black; one headline called Mentzel 'Mexican' [A3].

The Raton/Denver wire account of Mentzel's hanging ran in many papers [A2][A7][A8], and a separate Raton dispatch of June 28 reported Bradley's hanging [A14][A18]; all derive from the wire, and no local or official report was found.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Raton/Denver dispatch under crime headlines such as 'Bloody Affray—Three Men Killed and Others Wounded—The Murderer Lynched' and 'Hanged for Killing', without comment on the lynching.
The Bradley item was headed 'Followed His Pal', 'Served His Partner Likewise' and 'Bad Place for Gamblers', a light, approving tone toward the crowd's second hanging.
The Evening Critic headed its brief 'A Mexican Murderer Mobbed', the only paper to give Mentzel an ethnic label.

conflicts.note: The detailed Raton dispatch names three dead and lists Bergan as dying; later summaries likely counted Bergan, but no report of his death was found.
The detailed dispatch [A2] names a justice of the peace, a hotel proprietor and a saloon-keeper without saying whether they were helping the deputy.
